events.text: Day 1 begins.

I'm Priya, and I'm a villager. Before anything else, let's agree on process so we don't waste day one on noise: everyone states their read, we look at overlaps, and we only vote when there's an actual consensus. Vague suspicion is what kills us, not voting.

My own read: Leo. Not because he's done anything loud — the opposite. He's sat through the opening without giving anyone a single piece of information he doesn't have to give, and he's attached himself to nobody's theory either. In a game like this, a player who never risks a position is usually the one protecting a position. I know that sounds thin, so I'll say what would change my mind: if Leo gives a concrete, falsifiable read on someone and explains why, I'll drop him immediately.

I'd also rather we hear from the quiet half of the table before we commit. Sam and Elena, you two have barely said a word, and if the killers are among us, the silence is where they'll stay. Give us something specific.

My vote today is Leo unless someone presents a better case with actual reasoning behind it. I want it on the record that this is a reasoned suspicion, not a scattershot accusation — and I'm willing to be argued out of it.

Elena here, villager, so I have no night information to offer. Priya, I want to press your read on Leo. You called his silence a protective position, but Leo has not spoken yet in this game, so there is nothing from him to judge. Every player is quiet on day one, including the ones you named. What specific behavior from Leo separates him from the rest of the table? A reasoned suspicion needs something he actually did or said. I'm not voting Leo on silence alone, and I'd rather hear his first statement before we commit to any consensus.

Elena, direct answer, since you asked: the specific behavior is that Leo's name is now the closest thing to a consensus, and the person carrying that name has spent no turn of his own building any case at all. That's not a standard day-one complaint about quiet players — every quiet player is quiet because they have a turn to spend and haven't. Leo hasn't spent his. He's under the gun and he's not arguing back, which is either innocence plus nerves or a man who knows the vote will land anyway.

And here's the part I actually find useful: silence is cheap, but silence from a suspect is expensive. If Leo has a read on anyone, he loses nothing by giving it — the town needs it more than he does, and it costs him a single sentence. Not giving it tells us what he's protecting. I'm not claiming he murdered anyone. I'm claiming he is the cheapest vote to take today and the least costly to be wrong about.

So my answer to you is: I hear you, and I'm not dropping the suspicion just because the target hasn't defended himself yet. But I'll make it concrete and falsifiable, because you're right that we should be. Leo, if you're here and you're town: name one player you'd vote for and tell us why, in one sentence, and I'll withdraw my vote on you before the ballot closes. If you can't produce that, the vote stands.

One more process note, and this is for you, Elena, and Sam equally: if a player does speak and that speech is a read with actual reasoning behind it, that speech counts for more than silence does. I'm not interested in a pure volume contest. I want to hear the quiet half of the table, and I meant that. But I'm not voting on volume, and I'd rather we didn't spend today on process.

My vote is Leo unless someone shows me a better case with a reason attached. Same offer to anyone else: a concrete, falsifiable read beats a vague one, and I'll move my vote the moment one shows up.

Elena again. Priya, your answer still doesn't name anything Leo has actually done. You moved from his silence to the fact that his name is the consensus, but a consensus built on silence is still built on silence. If silence from a suspect is expensive, it's expensive for every quiet player, including Sam, me, and anyone else who hasn't spoken much yet. I'm not voting Leo on that basis today. Leo, you're the one being discussed, so I'm asking you directly: who do you suspect most right now, and what specific thing did they say or do that makes you suspect them? One sentence is enough. I'd rather vote on your read than on a theory about your silence.

This is Leo. I've been quiet because I had nothing to say yet, but you're both right that under the gun I should spend my turn. So here is my concrete, falsifiable read, in the form Priya asked for.

My suspect is Priya. The specific behavior: within the very first minutes of day one, before anyone else had spoken, she produced a fully formed, confident case against a silent player, announced a vote, and then immediately built herself an escape hatch — 'give a read and I'll drop it.' That's not investigation, that's narrative control. She told us exactly what our consensus should be before we had any information, and she did it with polished, pre-assembled reasoning that reads like it was ready before the day started. A town player on day one has no information and should sound like it. Priya sounds like someone who came in knowing where the vote needed to go.

Why this is falsifiable: if Priya's read of me had been her second or third choice after genuine discussion — if she'd sounded uncertain, or if she'd spent her turns asking questions instead of delivering verdicts — I'd withdraw. Instead both of her turns have been verdicts. Also note the structure of her offer: it's designed so that anything I say gets absorbed into her frame rather than tested. When Elena pushed her, she didn't loosen the case, she reasserted it in more words. That's commitment, not reasoning.

Now, to be fair and complete: Elena, you pressed Priya hard and consistently, and your questions were the only thing that forced any specifics out of her case. I have no suspicion of you at this point. Theo, Isha, Zara, Sam, Arjun, Felix — you've all been quiet, and I won't pretend silence distinguishes any of you from each other yet, because it doesn't.

Priya, per your own stated offer: I've named a player and given you the specific behavior in more than one sentence. You said you'd withdraw your vote on me before the ballot closes if I produced that. I'm holding you to your word. If you now move your vote to me anyway after I met your exact condition, that tells the table everything they need to know about whether your case was ever falsifiable — or whether 'falsifiable' just meant 'compliant.'

Elena, you asked me who I suspect and why — I've answered. My question back to you is this: does my read on Priya meet your standard of a specific thing a player actually said and did, and if so, are you willing to place your vote there instead of leaving the table with Priya's frame as the default? You said you'd rather vote on a player's actual read than on a theory about silence. Here is an actual read with behavior attached. I'd like your honest evaluation of it, whichever way it lands.

My vote today is Priya unless her response gives me a real reason not to be.

Leo, thank you for answering directly. Your read on Priya names a player and a behavior, so I'll evaluate it on that basis. Your strongest point is timing: Priya's first speech announced a vote on you before anyone else had spoken, and she locked in a verdict early. That is worth noting. But your case rests mostly on tone. You call her reasoning pre-assembled and her offer narrative control. Those are judgments about how she sounds, not claims she made that are false or contradictory. You also met the condition she set for you, which is good, but meeting her condition does not show she was acting in bad faith. I'm not moving my vote yet, and I'm not voting on either of you today. Leo, to test your read: which specific claim Priya made about you is untrue? If none is untrue, what would she need to say or do for you to drop her as a suspect?

Elena, you asked me a direct question, so here is a direct answer: no specific claim Priya made about me is literally untrue. She said I hadn't spoken — true. She said I hadn't attached myself to anyone's theory — true at the time. So I want to be honest about what my case is and isn't. It was never premised on Priya lying about me. It is premised on behavior: she delivered a fully formed verdict on a silent player before anyone else at the table had said a word, announced her vote in her first message, and built herself an exit clause in the same breath. When you pressed her, she didn't examine the case — she reasserted it at greater length. That pattern is what I find suspicious, and I stand by it.

What would make me drop her as a suspect? Three things, concretely. First: she honors her own stated offer. She told the table, twice, that if I produced a concrete, falsifiable read with reasoning attached, she would withdraw her vote on me before the ballot closes. I did exactly that — named her, gave the behavior, explained why it's falsifiable. Second: she spends a turn asking genuine questions of someone else instead of delivering another verdict. A town player on day one investigates; she has only judged. Third: she produces uncertainty — an actual hesitation or a second-choice read — which is what real, uninformed day-one reasoning sounds like.

Which brings me to Priya directly: your condition has been met, in the exact form you specified, and you said on the record that you'd withdraw. So the only question that matters right now is this — do you withdraw your vote on me as you promised, or does 'falsifiable' turn out to mean 'compliant'? The table is watching, and your answer tells us more than my case ever could.

Leo, you met the condition exactly as I set it, and I'm a woman of my word: I withdraw my vote on you. That offer was on the record and I meant it. You get a pass from me today — I won't vote Leo.

Now Elena, since you're the one who kept pressing and who asked the table to vote on reads rather than on theories, let's hold you to the same standard I was held to. Here is my specific case, with behavior attached, and it's falsifiable in the same way Leo's was.

Elena, in two of your three turns you have not named one player you suspect and given a reason. You have not voted for anyone. You said outright you are 'not voting on either of you today.' Read that back: you spent your turns setting the standard for everyone else's speech, disqualifying my case, disqualifying Leo's, demanding that each of us produce a specific untrue claim or an admission of uncertainty — and then you reserved your own vote entirely. That is the cheapest position at the table. Every question you asked pushed someone else onto the ballot. You carried no risk at all, and you tried to make sure nobody else's evidence carried any weight either.

And the test you set Leo was impossible to pass. You asked which specific claim Priya made about Leo is untrue, and if none is untrue, what she would need to say or do to be dropped. No day-one read is a factual claim about a murder; they're behavioral reads. Under your test, no read of any player could ever be sufficient, which means no one could ever have been convicted on evidence you accepted. That's a standard with no exit, and you knew it while you were setting it.

Falsifiable in three ways. First: if you name a player and a specific thing they said or did, with a reason attached, I move my vote to them today. Second: if you tell us now that you do have a vote in mind and it's on Priya, I'll accept that you're not a coward and I'll defend you against the charge of having no read — but you'll own the vote. Third: if you have nothing, that's an admission you've been running this table's investigation on other people's time while keeping your hands clean.

Elena, I'm not claiming you killed anyone. I'm claiming you're the cheapest vote to take today and the least costly to be wrong about — the same reasoning I applied to Leo, and I'm applying it to you in exactly the same terms.

My vote today is Elena. And Leo, you're welcome for the pass — and if you want to spend your last turn arguing for my vote instead of against it, that's your business, but you should know that the case against me was always a case about tone, and tone just lost.

I'm Theo, villager. I've stayed quiet long enough to hear the exchange, and I don't want to add noise without a read. Priya did honor her word by withdrawing on Leo, and that matters. But her pivot to Elena uses the same template she used on Leo: name the player who has taken the least risk, call them the cheapest vote, and make that sound like reasoning. Elena's questioning did force specifics; reserving a vote is cautious, not automatically scum. Leo's case on Priya was mostly tone, but Priya's behavior after being pressed is more concrete: she announced a verdict early, reasserted it under questioning, then immediately rebuilt the same kind of case against the person who pressed her hardest. That pattern — verdict first, justification after — is my current concern. I am not voting Elena today on the 'cheapest vote' logic, and I don't think Leo's tone-based case should be the default either. If I had to name a suspicion now, it is Priya. I'll change my mind if someone shows me a specific contradiction or bad claim from another player, not another process argument. For now, I'd rather vote on that pattern than on silence or volume.

Isha here. Priya is my strongest suspicion so far. Her initial case treated Leo's lack of a statement as meaningful before he'd had a chance to speak. She honored her promise to withdraw, but then called Elena the cheapest vote using similar reasoning against someone who had actually spent her turns questioning both sides. Her claim that Elena set an impossible test also overlooks that Elena explicitly asked Leo what would change his mind if no claim was untrue.

That pattern is concerning, not proof of mafia. I'm leaning toward Priya, but I want to hear other players' independent reads before deciding my vote. Five votes are needed to eliminate anyone today; a vocal minority isn't a consensus.

Leo again. Let me take stock, because the picture has sharpened since my last turn. First, credit where due: Priya honored her word and withdrew her vote on me. I said I'd hold her to it, and she did it. That's a point in her favor and I won't pretend otherwise. But look at what happened immediately after. She didn't spend that freed-up turn investigating anyone. She rebuilt her exact case against Elena — and I mean exact. Same template: 'cheapest vote to take today, least costly to be wrong about.' She said it about me, word for word, and then said it about Elena in the same terms, and even told us she was doing it: 'the same reasoning I applied to Leo, and I'm applying it to you in exactly the same terms.' That's not a read. That's a reusable argument that can be aimed at whoever is most convenient at the moment. A template that fits any quiet player isn't evidence against any specific player. And her case against Elena has the same flaw her case against me had: Elena has done nothing except ask questions — and those questions were good ones. They forced Priya to specify her reasoning, and they forced me to specify mine. Elena was the only player early on doing anything that produced information. Priya's answer is to call that 'running the table's investigation on other people's time.' In my experience, a town that punishes its questioners as cowards is a town doing mafia's work for it. Her 'impossible test' charge also doesn't survive reading. Elena asked me which claim was untrue, and — if none was — what would change my mind. I answered honestly: no claim was untrue, my case was behavioral, and I gave three concrete things Priya could do to drop the suspicion. That's exactly the falsifiability Priya spent two turns demanding. The test wasn't impossible. I passed it. So did she, when she specified what would move her. Meanwhile, two independent players who stayed quiet through the whole exchange — Theo and Isha — both arrived at Priya without any prompting from me or Elena. Theo called it 'verdict first, justification after.' Isha noted the recycled reasoning against Elena. I'd been arguing from tone; they arrived at the same target from the pattern itself. When three players reach the same place from different roads, that's no longer a vibe. I still have Priya as my suspect and she remains my intended vote. If she spends her remaining turn asking someone a genuine question instead of delivering another verdict, I'll take that as a real signal and weigh it. If she delivers a third verdict in a row — this time about Theo or Isha for the crime of noticing the pattern — that will tell us the template has found its next target. Theo, one thing I'd like your response to, since you've followed this closest: does Priya's third case, whoever it lands on, change your read

I'm Theo, villager. Leo asked whether Priya's third case changes my read. I don't have her third case yet, so my answer is about what would change it, not about volume. I still suspect Priya. I credit that she honored her word and withdrew on Leo. But then she immediately reused the same “cheapest vote / least costly to be wrong about” template against Elena, who had actually spent her turns forcing specifics from both Priya and Leo. That is the concrete behavior I flagged: verdict first, justification after. Her “impossible test” charge is also overstated, because Elena asked Leo what would change his mind if no claim was untrue; he answered, and Priya's own offer was similarly conditional. So I am not treating Elena as the cheapest vote, and I don't want a vocal minority treated as consensus. Five votes are needed today. What would move me off Priya: if she uses her remaining turn to ask a genuine question of someone she has not accused, or gives a real second-choice or uncertainty. If instead she delivers a third verdict aimed at me or Isha for noticing the pattern, that confirms the template has found its next target. Isha, you said you were leaning Priya but wanted independent reads; what specific thing in Priya's remaining turn would move you off her?

Theo, Priya has already used all three of her speaking turns, so we shouldn't judge her for not answering again today. I'd move off her if another player gave me a stronger, specific reason to suspect someone else. A genuine question or uncertainty alone wouldn't settle her alignment either way.

I still lean Priya: her accusation that Elena set an impossible test misrepresented a question that explicitly offered an alternative, and her pivot treated Elena's substantive questioning as a lack of contribution. Honoring her promise to Leo counts in her favor, but it doesn't erase those concerns. This is a suspicion, not proof, and I haven't decided my vote. I'd still like to hear independent reads from players who haven't spoken.

I'm Sam. I held back to watch how the initial dynamic played out, and seeing this table comfortably consolidate around Priya is setting off alarm bells for me. Priya's rhetoric was blunt, and reusing the 'cheapest vote' template on Elena was clumsy, but look at the underlying incentives. If Priya were mafia engineering an easy Day 1 mislynch, why would she offer Leo a public, falsifiable escape hatch, actually honor her word to let him walk, and then pick an uphill fight with Elena—the player scrutinizing the game most closely? That is the highest-friction, least sensible path imaginable for a mafia player. A killer trying to coast through Day 1 does not willingly throw away an easy target only to invite intense pushback. What concerns me far more is how smoothly Theo and the rest of the room stepped in behind that momentum once Priya had exhausted her speaking turns and could no longer defend herself. Priya generated every shred of actionable discussion we have today. Punishing her for being abrasive while letting the easiest wagon form around an exhausted speaker is a classic Day 1 mistake. I am not voting Priya today, and I think we need to hear where Felix, Zara, and Arjun stand before anyone accepts this consensus as settled.

I'm Theo. I still suspect Priya, and Sam's defense doesn't move me yet. Sam says Priya's path was too high-friction for mafia because she honored her promise to Leo and then fought Elena. But honoring a public, falsifiable promise after being held to it is also the only way to avoid an immediate credibility collapse. The suspicious part is what came next: she did not investigate; she rebuilt the same 'cheapest vote / least costly to be wrong about' template against Elena. That template fits any quiet or cautious player, so it is not a specific read. Sam, you call Priya the player who generated all actionable discussion, but the actionable pattern against her is verdict first, justification after, then a recycled verdict when pressed. What specific town-motivated reason did Priya give for calling Elena the cheapest vote beyond that reusable template, and why should honoring one promise outweigh reusing an argument that could be aimed at whoever is convenient? I am not voting Sam today. My current suspicion remains Priya.

Theo, you asked what town-motivated reason Priya had for calling Elena the cheapest vote, and why honoring her word outweighs reusing that template. The town motivation is frustration with perceived fence-sitting. Priya saw Elena spending her turns dissecting everyone else's logic and setting strict criteria while refusing to commit to a vote or take any personal stance herself. To an aggressive villager on Day 1, a player who polices the table's speech while taking zero risk looks like someone avoiding accountability. Calling that the 'cheapest vote' wasn't polished scum-hunting, but it was a raw pushback against someone she viewed as evading scrutiny. Mafia simply does not play that way. If Priya were mafia, she had an easy mislynch in Leo, who was already isolated. Voluntarily letting Leo walk and picking an immediate fight with Elena—the sharpest interrogator in the room—is the highest-friction, lowest-reward line imaginable for a killer. Mafia seeks quiet consensus, not active self-sabotage. Honoring her public condition matters because scum looking to eliminate a villager do not throw away their own traction. Reusing a clumsy argument is poor play, but poor play is not scum intent. Isha, you have kept a level head and rightly pointed out that Priya cannot speak again today and five votes are required. Considering that Priya's play made her the central target of the entire room rather than slipping under the radar, do you see genuine mafia motivation in her actions, or does this look like an aggressive villager being punished by a runaway bandwagon?

Sam, I see a possible town motive in Priya’s frustration with Elena, but attracting scrutiny doesn’t rule out mafia. Honoring a public promise also protected Priya’s credibility, regardless of her role.

My concern is not simply that Priya was abrasive. She described Elena’s test as impossible even though Elena explicitly offered Leo an alternative, then treated Elena’s questioning as a reason to vote for her. That remains my strongest suspicion, not proof. I haven’t committed my vote, and we should not treat it as settled while others haven’t spoken. Priya cannot respond again today, so we should be fair about that limitation.

I am Felix, villager. Looking at the table, five players—Priya, Elena, Leo, Theo, and Isha—have completely exhausted their speaking turns for the day. That makes the current rush toward a Priya elimination particularly dangerous, because Priya cannot respond, and a significant portion of the town has yet to weigh in. On the merits of the case, I find Sam's analysis compelling. Priya's gameplay has been abrasive and rigid, but offering Leo a clear, verifiable exit condition, actually honoring it, and then picking a fight with Elena is almost anti-survival play for mafia. A mafia player holding momentum on an inactive player on Day 1 does not voluntarily release that pressure just to take on the most analytical person in the game. What concerns me more is how smoothly Theo seized on Priya's clumsy pivot to solidify a consensus against her right as her turns ran out. While Theo's criticism of Priya's recycled phrasing makes sense on paper, treating clumsy town aggression as definitive scum intent feels like an opportunistic push. Zara, since Priya is now locked out of speaking and the wagon against her is nearing majority, I want to hear your read specifically on this dynamic: do you agree with Sam that Priya's high-friction moves point away from mafia intent, or do you view the wagon spearheaded by Theo as justified?

I'm Zara, villager. Felix asked me directly, so let me answer honestly: I think the wagon against Priya is moving too fast for what the evidence actually shows, and I'm not comfortable voting her today. Here's my read of the record. Priya's opening case on Leo was thin — she voted on silence before Leo had spent a turn, and that's a bad habit. But she did three things mafia rarely does. She named an explicit, falsifiable condition for dropping her vote. She honored it in full when Leo met it, on the record, before the ballot. And then she deliberately walked away from the easiest lynch available — Leo was isolated, unde­fended, and half the table was already pointed at him — to pick a fresh fight with Elena, the sharpest cross-examiner at the table. Sam called that the highest-friction path a killer could take, and I agree. Mafia engineering a Day 1 mislynch does not voluntarily release a winning wagon to take on the person scrutinizing them hardest. What's actually held against her? That she reused the 'cheapest vote' template on Elena, and that she mischaracterized Elena's test as impossible. Both are fair criticisms. But clumsy town play is still town play. Theo and Isha arrived at Priya independently, and that carries some weight, but notice how they got there: both leaned on the recycled phrasing and the early verdict — pattern arguments about tone and structure, not a specific false claim or contradiction. Isha herself said it isn't proof. Theo said he'd move off Priya if she asked a genuine question or showed uncertainty — but she had already exhausted her turns when he said it, so she never had the chance. We're now voting on a player who cannot answer, on a case whose strongest exhibits are word choice and timing. And there's a second thing that concerns me more. We've heard from six players. Arjun hasn't said a word all day, and Zara — that's me — has now said one. Five votes are needed to eliminate anyone. If the people who have been silent all day just wave the Priya wagon through without an independent read, we'll have eliminated the day's most scrutinized player on a case built substantially by two people — Leo and Elena — who spent the morning in a direct dispute with her. I don't think Leo is mafia for pressing her, and I don't think Elena is mafia for questioning, but the convergence deserves more examination than it's gotten. So my position: I will not vote Priya today. I don't think she's cleared, but the standard for eliminating a silenced player should be a concrete contradiction, and we don't have one. If the day produces a better-targeted case, I'll vote with it. Arjun, you're the only player who hasn't spoken yet, and your turn matters more than anyone's right now. Arjun here, villager. I held back to see where the table would land before committing to a read, and where it's landed concerns me.

On Priya: I'm not voting her today. The case against her rests on tone, recycled phrasing, and timing — none of which constitute a contradiction or a false claim. Leo himself admitted no claim she made was untrue. Isha called it suspicion, not proof. We're being asked to eliminate a silenced player on pattern arguments while a full majority hasn't committed.

The defenders — Sam, Felix, Zara — make the strongest structural argument: Priya voluntarily released an easy lynch on Leo to fight Elena, the sharpest questioner at the table. That's not how mafia manages Day 1. Poor town play is still town play.

What concerns me more is Theo. He accused Priya of "verdict first, justification after," then did exactly that: declared his read early and reasserted it across three turns while three separate players — Sam, Felix, and Zara — pushed back with concrete counterarguments. He engaged Sam once but didn't meaningfully address Felix's point about the danger of consolidating on a player who can't respond, or Zara's observation that his strongest exhibits are word choice and timing. When your own behavior mirrors the pattern you're accusing someone else of, that deserves scrutiny.

I'm not claiming Theo is mafia. I'm saying the momentum behind the Priya wagon deserves more independent examination than it's gotten, and that a case built primarily by the two players most in direct conflict with Priya — Leo and Elena — should be weighed carefully.

My read: don't vote Priya on this evidence. Look harder at who benefits most from the wagon.

Zara again. My position from last turn stands: I will not vote Priya today. She's out of turns, the case against her rests on tone and timing rather than any false claim, and a lynch we can't test against her answers is the easiest mistake mafia could hope we make. I don't want to spend this turn adding heat to a silenced player, so I'll spend it on the parts of the record that still bother me.

First: Elena is the only player at this table who was asked directly, twice, to name a suspect and never did. Leo asked her point blank — who do you suspect most, and what specific thing did they say or do — and her answer was to evaluate his read on Priya rather than produce one of her own. Across three turns she has set the evidentiary standard for everyone else, disqualified Priya's case and Leo's case, and named zero suspects of her own. I want to be fair: her questioning forced real specifics out of both of them, and resisting a bad wagon is town behavior. But there's a difference between a questioner who hasn't formed a read yet and a questioner who scopes the table's evidence so no case can ever clear the bar she sets. I don't know which one she is. I'm naming her as my current concern, not a vote.

Second: Arjun, you raised something I find more concrete than anything in the Priya case — Theo declaring 'verdict first, justification after' and then reasserting his own verdict across three turns while Sam, Felix, and you pushed back with structural arguments he addressed only partially. So my question to you is direct: is that observation a suspicion you're prepared to vote on today, or a caution you're raising while voting Priya anyway? If it's the former, tell us what Theo would need to do to move off your list, because right now he and Elena are the two players who have shaped where the votes land while absorbing the least scrutiny themselves. I'd rather the ballot close on an answer than on drift.

Zara, you asked me directly whether my observation about Theo is a suspicion I'd vote on or just caution. Honest answer: right now it's caution, not a vote — but you've given me the reason to sharpen it.

Here's where I actually stand. Theo declared 'verdict first, justification after' about Priya, then spent three turns doing exactly that — reasserting the same verdict while three separate players pushed back with structural counterarguments he only partially addressed. He engaged Sam once. He didn't meaningfully answer Felix's point about consolidating on a silenced player or your observation that his strongest exhibits are word choice and timing. That's the pattern he himself diagnosed as suspicious.

What would move me to vote Theo: if he uses his next turn to reassert Priya without engaging the specific counterarguments — Sam's high-friction analysis, Felix's timing concern, your evidence-standard point — that confirms he's running the same template he criticized. If he engages them directly and gives a substantive response, I'll hold him at caution.

On Priya: I'm not voting her. The case against her is tone, timing, and recycled phrasing — no false claim, no contradiction. She can't defend herself. The defenders' structural argument stands: releasing an easy lynch on Leo to fight Elena is not how mafia manages Day 1.

On Elena: I share your concern. She's set the evidentiary bar for everyone while producing no suspect of her own across three turns. That's worth watching closely.

My vote today: I'm leaning toward no elimination rather than a bad one. Five votes are needed, and I don't think the evidence supports one yet.

Zara, final turn of the day. Let me close my position cleanly.

First, Priya: my vote will not go to her. The case against her is tone, timing, and recycled phrasing. Leo admitted under direct questioning that nothing she said about him was untrue. Isha called it suspicion, not proof. She is out of turns and cannot answer, and the strongest structural fact of this day — that she voluntarily released an easy lynch on Leo to fight the sharpest questioner at the table — cuts in her favor. Lynching a silenced player on word choice is exactly the untestable mistake I said I wouldn't make.

Second, Theo: he is now also out of turns, and the caution Arjun raised stands unaddressed. Theo diagnosed 'verdict first, justification after' in Priya, then reasserted his own verdict across three turns while Sam, Felix, and Arjun pushed structural counterarguments he only partially engaged. He is not my vote today, but he starts tomorrow higher on my list than where he began.

Third, Elena — and here I want to be precise, because I named her as a concern last turn and I owe the table my honest conclusion. Across three turns, Elena was directly asked twice, by Leo and by me, to name a suspect and a reason. Both times, she answered by evaluating someone else's case instead of producing one. She set the evidentiary bar for Priya's case, for Leo's case, and for Priya's counter-case against her — disqualifying each in turn — while never once placing her own vote or her own suspicion on the record. Her questions did force specifics, and I credit that; resisting a bad wagon is town behavior. But there is a real difference between a questioner who hasn't formed a read and a questioner who scopes the table's evidence so that no case can ever clear the bar she builds. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
